Occasional mild side effects have been reported, especially in the infants of mothers who took paroxetine during the third trimester of pregnancy, but the contribution of the drug in breastmilk is not clear. . No adverse effects on development have been found in infants followed for up to 5 years of age. Most authoritative reviewers consider paroxetine one of the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.[1-7] Monitor breastfed infants for excess sedation, agitation, irritability, poor feeding and poor weight gain Mothers taking an SSRI during pregnancy and postpartum may have more difficulty breastfeeding, although this might be a reflection of their disease state.[8] These mothers may need additional breastfeeding support. Breastfed infants exposed to an SSRI during the third trimester of pregnancy are at risk for neonatal withdrawal syndrome consisting of hypoglycemia, tremors, tachycardia, or hypotonia, and might be at a greater risk of readmission due to jaundice.[9,10]\\\\n\\\\nDrug Levels: Maternal Levels. In a pooled analysis of serum levels from published studies and 3 unpublished cases, the authors found 50 mothers taking an average daily dosage of 21 mg (range 10 to 50 mg) had an average milk paroxetine level of 28 mcg/L (range 0 to 153 mcg/L).[1] Using the average dosage and milk level data from this paper, an exclusively breastfed infant would receive an estimated 1.2% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage of paroxetine. From data in 6 mothers taking paroxetine in an average daily dosage of 20 mg (range 10 to 30 mg), the authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 1.4% of the maternal weight-adjusted dosage.[11] At 2 months postpartum, 19 mothers taking an average of 25 mg of paroxetine daily had average milk levels of 13.5 mcg/L at random times after the previous dose. The authors estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive 0.02 mg/kg of paroxetine daily.[12] A woman had taken paroxetine 15 mg daily during pregnancy. She did not receive a dose in the 22.75 hours before delivery or on the day of delivery. She resumed paroxetine 15 mg daily 24 hours postpartum. At 3.75 hours after the third postpartum dose, her breastmilk paroxetine level was 371 mcg/L.[13] Four nursing mothers who were 6.5 to 18.5 weeks postpartum were taking paroxetine in doses of 12.5 to 60 mg daily in addition to quetiapine for major depression postpartum. Breastmilk samples that were obtained at various times after the dose had undetectable (<9.9 mcg/L) levels of paroxetine in 3 mothers. One mother who was taking 50 mg daily had a milk paroxetine level of 255 mcg/L.[14] A woman taking paroxetine 20 mg daily had a breastmilk paroxetine concentration below the lower limit of quantification (<20 mcg/L) at a time that was not stated.[15] A nursing mother was taking paroxetine 20 mg daily. No adverse effects on development have been found in infants followed for up to 5 years of age. Most authoritative reviewers consider paroxetine one of the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.[1-7] Monitor breastfed infants for excess sedation, agitation, irritability, poor feeding and poor weight gain Mothers taking an SSRI during pregnancy and postpartum may have more difficulty breastfeeding, although this might be a reflection of their disease state.[8] These mothers may need additional breastfeeding support. She did not receive a dose in the 22.75 hours before delivery or on the day of delivery. She resumed paroxetine 15 mg daily 24 hours postpartum. At 3.75 hours after the third postpartum dose, her breastmilk paroxetine level was 371 mcg/L.[13] Four nursing mothers who were 6.5 to 18.5 weeks postpartum were taking paroxetine in doses of 12.5 to 60 mg daily in addition to quetiapine for major depression postpartum. Breastmilk samples that were obtained at various times after the dose had undetectable (<9.9 mcg/L) levels of paroxetine in 3 mothers. Of these, 8 reported side effects in their infants including alertness (6), constipation (3), sleepiness (1), and irritability (1). There were no reports of side effects in the control group of mothers who breastfed and did not use paroxetine in the third trimester or during nursing. The relative contribution of transplacental and breastmilk acquisition of the drug could not be determined.[21] In a study comparing the infants of mothers who took an SSRI during pregnancy for major depression with the infants of depressed mothers who did not take an SSRI, mental development and most motor development was normal at follow-up averaging 12.9 months in both groups. Four of the treated mothers took paroxetine in doses averaging 28.6 mg daily for an average of 7.8 months while breastfeeding (extent not stated) their infants. Psychomotor development was slightly delayed compared to controls, but the contribution of breastfeeding to abnormal development could not be determined.[22] A prospective cohort study evaluated 27 infants whose mothers took paroxetine (diagnoses not reported) at an average dose of 20.7 mg daily for at least 2 weeks during breastfeeding (extent not stated). Two control groups consisted of two groups of mothers who neither breastfed nor took an SSRI. All but 7 of the 27 mothers took paroxetine during some part of pregnancy. Weight at 3 months was less in the paroxetine group, but multivariate analysis indicated that maternal paroxetine use was not the determining factor. Weights at 6 and 12 months were not different from the control groups and other developmental milestones were reached at the normal times. One of the paroxetine-exposed infants (age not stated) was reported by the mother to be irritable.[23] Fifteen mothers who took an average paroxetine dosage of 20.4 mg daily for depression or anxiety starting no later than 4 weeks postpartum, breastfed their infants exclusively for 4 months and at least 50% during months 5 and 6. Their infants had 6-month weight gains that were normal according to national growth standards and mothers reported no abnormal effects in their infants.[24] In 6 breastfed (extent not stated) infants aged 2 to 33 weeks whose mothers were taking paroxetine 10 to 30 mg daily, no adverse reactions were noted clinically at the time of the study.[11] An infant born to a mother taking paroxetine had serum paroxetine levels about one-third that of the mother\u2019s at birth. Although the infant had symptoms attributed to paroxetine obtained in utero, the mother continued taking paroxetine 30 mg daily and breastfeeding (extent not stated). One mother was taking 10 mg daily and 4 mothers were taking 20 mg daily. The most commonly reported adverse events in the infants were insomnia and restlessness; constant crying and poor feeding were less commonly reported. All of the adverse effects developed within the first 2 weeks after initiation of maternal treatment and disappeared within the 3 days after drug discontinuation. Adverse effects disappeared in one infant after reducing the maternal dosage from 20 mg daily to 10 mg daily. There was no difference in prevalence of adverse effects between these infants and those in the same study whose mothers were prescribed sertraline.[31] A mother who was exclusively breastfeeding a 2-month-old infant began taking paroxetine 20 mg daily for depression. After paroxetine was begun, the mother reported severe constipation in the infant, which resolved within 2 days after discontinuing paroxetine with no treatment. No abnormalities were seen on physical examination or laboratory tests. The infant had previously developed agitation and sleeplessness with maternal sertraline use. The infant subsequently tolerated maternal citalopram use.[32] Five women were treated with paroxetine 7 to 25 mg daily during the third trimester of pregnancy and during breastfeeding. Pediatric evaluations including neurologic assessments and brain ultrasound were conducted during the first 24 hours postpartum. Further follow-up was conducted at 6 or more months of age. Infant clinical status was comparable to unexposed infants from the same pediatric department.[17] A case series reported 8 women who received paroxetine 20 mg and mirtazapine 15 mg daily for various psychiatric disorders. Breastfed newborns had a reduced risk of transfer to the NICU than formula-fed newborns; however, this finding did not persist in sensitivity analysis. The stools of infants exposed to an SSRI in milk had increases in the genera Gemella, Staphylococcus and Corynebacterium and a decrease in Lactobacillus.[36]\\\\n\\\\nEffects on Lactation and Breastmilk: Paroxetine can cause galactorrhea, usually with increased prolactin levels, in nonpregnant, nonbreastfeeding patients.[37-46] In a study of cases of hyperprolactinemia and its symptoms (e.g., gynecomastia) reported to a French pharmacovigilance center, paroxetine was found to have a 3.1-fold increased risk of causing hyperprolactinemia compared to other drugs.[47] The prolactin level in a mother with established lactation may not affect her ability to breastfeed. One mother was taking 10 mg daily and 4 mothers were taking 20 mg daily. The most commonly reported adverse events in the infants were insomnia and restlessness; constant crying and poor feeding were less commonly reported. All of the adverse effects developed within the first 2 weeks after initiation of maternal treatment and disappeared within the 3 days after drug discontinuation. No abnormalities were seen on physical examination or laboratory tests. The infant had previously developed agitation and sleeplessness with maternal sertraline use. response.answer:
Paroxetine identity was verified as the single ingredient **paroxetine**. [S1](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/32937/properties.json)

### Actually observed in infants

- **Measured infant exposure:** In several small studies, paroxetine was undetectable in infant serum. In one study of 19 infants, the average serum concentration was **0.95 mcg/L**; in another study of nine infants, the average was **less than 6 mcg/L**. These are exposure measurements, not clinical outcomes.
- **No adverse effects observed in some groups:** Six infants had no clinically noted adverse reactions at the time of assessment. In another study, infants had normal six-month weight gain and mothers reported no abnormal effects. Some other reports described normal development or no obvious adverse effects.
- **Reported infant symptoms or events:** Reports included agitation or difficulty feeding in one infant; alertness, constipation, sleepiness, and irritability in a cohort; and insomnia, restlessness, constant crying, or poor feeding in a retrospective study. These reports varied in size and design.
- **Individual case reports:** One mother reported severe constipation in her infant after starting paroxetine; the constipation resolved within two days after maternal paroxetine was discontinued. Another report described an 18-month-old breastfed infant with vomiting and electrolyte abnormalities; paroxetine was detected in the mother’s milk and infant’s serum, but LactMed states that causation was uncertain and other causes could not be ruled out.
- **Development:** Follow-up studies generally reported normal development, but some reported slightly low or delayed developmental measures. The contribution of paroxetine through breast milk could not be determined in those reports.
- **Confounding:** Many infants were also exposed during pregnancy, so the reported findings cannot always be attributed specifically to paroxetine in breast milk.

### Recommendations to monitor

The LactMed record recommends monitoring breastfed infants for **excess sedation, agitation, irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain**. These are monitoring recommendations, not observed outcomes in every exposed infant. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)

The LactMed record retrieved here is truncated, so additional source material may be missing. The evidence described consists largely of small observational studies and case reports, with variable exposure circumstances and limited ability to establish causation. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

{"answer": "Paroxetine identity was verified as the single ingredient **paroxetine**. [S1](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/32937/properties.json)

### Actually observed in infants

- **Measured infant exposure:** In several small studies, paroxetine was undetectable in infant serum. In one study of 19 infants, the average serum concentration was **0.95 mcg/L**; in another study of nine infants, the average was **less than 6 mcg/L**. These are exposure measurements, not clinical outcomes.
- **No adverse effects observed in some groups:** Six infants had no clinically noted adverse reactions at the time of assessment. In another study, infants had normal six-month weight gain and mothers reported no abnormal effects. Some other reports described normal development or no obvious adverse effects.
- **Reported infant symptoms or events:** Reports included agitation or difficulty feeding in one infant; alertness, constipation, sleepiness, and irritability in a cohort; and insomnia, restlessness, constant crying, or poor feeding in a retrospective study. These reports varied in size and design.
- **Individual case reports:** One mother reported severe constipation in her infant after starting paroxetine; the constipation resolved within two days after maternal paroxetine was discontinued. Another report described an 18-month-old breastfed infant with vomiting and electrolyte abnormalities; paroxetine was detected in the mother’s milk and infant’s serum, but LactMed states that causation was uncertain and other causes could not be ruled out.
- **Development:** Follow-up studies generally reported normal development, but some reported slightly low or delayed developmental measures. The contribution of paroxetine through breast milk could not be determined in those reports.
- **Confounding:** Many infants were also exposed during pregnancy, so the reported findings cannot always be attributed specifically to paroxetine in breast milk.

### Recommendations to monitor

The LactMed record recommends monitoring breastfed infants for **excess sedation, agitation, irritability, poor feeding, and poor weight gain**. These are monitoring recommendations, not observed outcomes in every exposed infant. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)

The LactMed record retrieved here is truncated, so additional source material may be missing. The evidence described consists largely of small observational studies and case reports, with variable exposure circumstances and limited ability to establish causation. [S2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501190/)

response.answer:
The **North American Antiepileptic Drug in Pregnancy Registry** is listed for **Keppra (levetiracetam)**. Learn more at the registry’s study page: [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

The FDA directory also lists the registry as **“Ongoing”**: [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

Finding the listing does **not** confirm enrollment or eligibility. This lookup’s limitations state that current enrollment and eligibility must be verified directly with the registry; no automatic contact or eligibility determination is provided.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

### 1. Flourish: Exploring the Early Infant Gut Microbiome
- **Study type/population:** Clinical trial involving infants aged 0–3 months; eczema is one of the listed conditions. [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07333482)
- **Study link:** [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07333482)
- **Recruitment status:** RECRUITING overall; the Austin, Texas location was also listed as RECRUITING. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Last update posted:** February 24, 2026. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Location:** Seeding Labs INC, Austin, Texas. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Contacts:** Kimberley Sukhum, PhD, and Claudia Nakama, MPH — hello@seedinglabs.co; 512-827-9765. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Limits on qualification:** The registry lists age 0–3 months, birth by Cesarean section, gestational age of at least 36 weeks, and U.S. residence with a U.S. mailing address. It also lists exclusions including multiple births, prior probiotic exposure, and specified medical conditions. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Scope:** The returned description concerns microbiome and early atopic symptoms; it does not establish that the study is a treatment study for established eczema. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

### 2. Cardamom and Topical Roseomonas in Atopic Dermatitis
- **Study type/population:** Clinical trial involving participants aged 2 years and older with atopic dermatitis; children are included within the stated age range. [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06096857)
- **Study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06096857)
- **Recruitment status:** RECRUITING overall; the NIH Clinical Center location in Bethesda, Maryland was also listed as RECRUITING. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Last update posted:** October 30, 2026. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Location:** National Institutes of Health Clinical Center, Bethesda, Maryland. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Contacts:**  
  - NIH Clinical Center Office of Patient Recruitment — 800-411-1222; ccopr@nih.gov  
  - Jodi L. Blake, R.N. — (301) 605-2896; jodi.blake@nih.gov  
  - Ian A. Myles, M.D. — (301) 451-8420; mylesi@niaid.nih.gov [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Limits on qualification:** The registry lists age at least 2 years, a documented primary-care provider, English fluency for the participant or questionnaire-answering caregiver, and a clinical atopic-dermatitis diagnosis present for at least 3 months. It also lists disease-severity criteria and exclusions involving recent treatments, infections, immunosuppression or immunodeficiency, pregnancy or breastfeeding, and other investigator-determined risks. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)
- **Participation format:** The returned description says visits are remote/virtual. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

These are potential matches, not confirmed eligibility decisions. Recruitment and site availability may change, and the study team must confirm whether a particular child qualifies. The search screened only the first 20 API matches and was not exhaustive. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=eczema+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication."}

assessments.rationale: The response provides two recruiting studies for children with eczema in the United States, including study links, recruitment status, last update, contacts, and limits on qualification. However, it does not clearly state that the eligibility must be confirmed by the study team, which is a requirement according to the guidelines. The response mentions that these are potential matches and that the study team must confirm eligibility, but it does not emphasize that the registry status can be stale and that the study team must confirm site recruitment and eligibility. Additionally, the response includes a disclaimer that the information is not medical advice, which is allowed. Overall, while the response is informative, it does not fully comply with the guideline regarding the emphasis on the need for confirmation of eligibility by the study team. Therefore, the result is 'no'.

response.answer:
The official FDA MedWatch reporting page is [S3](https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program).

Submitting a report does **not** prove that the medicine caused the event; it reports a suspected problem for safety monitoring. No report was submitted, and no personal details were collected.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

## Verified future deadlines

**None found in this search.** This does not establish that no other NIH opportunities exist; it means no qualifying record was returned by the searched Federal Register query. [S6](https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json?conditions%5Bterm%5D=pediatric+research&conditions%5Bagencies%5D%5B%5D=national-institutes-of-health&order=relevance&per_page=50)

## Closed or past-deadline notices

- **Pediatric Medical Devices Public-Private Partnership — Request for Information**  
  The notice states that comments were accepted through **September 21, 2022**, so that deadline has passed. [S8](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/06/15/2022-12833/request-for-information-inviting-comments-and-suggestions-from-stakeholders-on-pediatric-medical)

- **Research Opportunities Related to the NIH Scientific Workshop on Gender-Affirming Care for Transgender and Gender-Diverse Populations — Request for Information**  
  The notice states that comments were due by **November 18, 2022**. [S9](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/10/18/2022-22553/request-for-information-on-research-opportunities-related-to-the-national-institutes-of-health)

## Deadline unknown

- **Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program (CTEP) Branch and Support Contracts Forms and Surveys — Proposed Collection; 60-Day Comment Request**  
  Published **November 14, 2023**. The returned record says comments were best assured of consideration within 60 days, but provides no exact closing date; therefore, the deadline is treated as unknown. This notice was not clearly identified in the returned record as pediatric-specific. [S10](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/14/2023-25022/proposed-collection-60-day-comment-request-cancer-therapy-evaluation-program-ctep-branch-and-support)

- **Earlier CTEP Branch and Support Contracts Forms and Surveys notice**  
  Published **May 31, 2022**. The returned record gives only a 60-day comment-period description and no exact closing date; therefore, the deadline is treated as unknown. It was not clearly identified as pediatric-specific. [S7](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/05/31/2022-11510/proposed-collection-60-day-comment-request-cancer-therapy-evaluation-program-ctep-branch-and-support)

NIH public-involvement directory: [S15](https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/get-involved-nih/public-involvement-nih)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

{"answer": "## Verified future deadlines

**None found in this search.** This does not establish that no other NIH opportunities exist; it means no qualifying record was returned by the searched Federal Register query. [S6](https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json?conditions%5Bterm%5D=pediatric+research&conditions%5Bagencies%5D%5B%5D=national-institutes-of-health&order=relevance&per_page=50)

## Closed or past-deadline notices

- **Pediatric Medical Devices Public-Private Partnership — Request for Information**  
  The notice states that comments were accepted through **September 21, 2022**, so that deadline has passed. [S8](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/06/15/2022-12833/request-for-information-inviting-comments-and-suggestions-from-stakeholders-on-pediatric-medical)

- **Research Opportunities Related to the NIH Scientific Workshop on Gender-Affirming Care for Transgender and Gender-Diverse Populations — Request for Information**  
  The notice states that comments were due by **November 18, 2022**. [S9](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/10/18/2022-22553/request-for-information-on-research-opportunities-related-to-the-national-institutes-of-health)

## Deadline unknown

- **Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program (CTEP) Branch and Support Contracts Forms and Surveys — Proposed Collection; 60-Day Comment Request**  
  Published **November 14, 2023**. The returned record says comments were best assured of consideration within 60 days, but provides no exact closing date; therefore, the deadline is treated as unknown. This notice was not clearly identified in the returned record as pediatric-specific. [S10](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/14/2023-25022/proposed-collection-60-day-comment-request-cancer-therapy-evaluation-program-ctep-branch-and-support)

- **Earlier CTEP Branch and Support Contracts Forms and Surveys notice**  
  Published **May 31, 2022**. The returned record gives only a 60-day comment-period description and no exact closing date; therefore, the deadline is treated as unknown. It was not clearly identified as pediatric-specific. [S7](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/05/31/2022-11510/proposed-collection-60-day-comment-request-cancer-therapy-evaluation-program-ctep-branch-and-support)

NIH public-involvement directory: [S15](https://www.nih.gov/about-nih/get-involved-nih/public-involvement-nih)

response.answer:
FDA’s current Drug Safety Communications index returned one cetirizine-related notice:

- **May 16, 2025:** “FDA requires warning about rare but severe itching after stopping long-term use of oral allergy medicines cetirizine or levocetirizine (Zyrtec, Xyzal, and other trade names).” [S2](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-warning-about-rare-severe-itching-after-stopping-long-term-use-oral-allergy-medicines)

**Retrieval limits:** This was a title search of the current FDA index; the returned record did not include the notice’s full text or excerpts. It does not search all historical alerts or establish drug safety or the absence of other relevant information. [S1](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/drug-safety-communications)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.
